summary:
Fire behaves completely differently in space than it does on Earth, and guessing how a material will burn inside a spacecraft or lunar habitat can put crews at risk. We built AstraFlame, an interactive 3D combustion lab and research workbench grounded in NASA's BASS-II, Saffire, and LUCI flight data.

Instead of making up predictions when data is missing, AstraFlame checks every user configuration against 78 mapped NASA flight records and 55 quarantined legacy rows. If you test an unstudied condition, like a 34% oxygen lunar habitat, the Physics Domain Safety Gate stops and shows exactly which variables lack flight evidence.

Researchers and students can explore a 3D BASS-II flow duct, inspect flame imagery in Flame Vision, look up source-verified answers in Ask AURA, and complete 5 hands-on missions.
details:
What AstraFlame Does and How It Works

AstraFlame turns NASA’s microgravity combustion research (BASS, BASS-II, Saffire IV–VI, and LUCI lunar-gravity drop-tower tests) into an interactive web workbench where users can explore real spacecraft fire behavior without guesswork.

Instead of acting like a black-box simulator that always spits out an answer, every tool in AstraFlame runs through a Physics Domain Safety Gate and a strict evidence ledger:

  • 3D Flame Lab (/lab): Users adjust gravity (Earth 1 g, Mars 0.38 g, Moon 0.17 g, or ISS microgravity), oxygen concentration (10–40%), duct airflow, pressure, and material (PMMA, SIBAL cotton/fiberglass, Nomex, Silicone, Cotton jersey). A Three.js WebGL BASS-II flow duct visualizes the flame with an optional IR false-color view, live thermocouple/radiometer/O₂ telemetry traces, a local run Notebook with CSV export, and a fair-test comparator. Whenever a setup leaves the bounds of NASA’s flight data (for example, an untested 34% O₂ lunar habitat), the gate abstains and explains which variable lacks evidence.
  • Experiment Atlas & Evidence Workstation (/atlas, /dashboard, /model-lab): Maps 78 NASA flight and suborbital test records on an interactive O₂-vs-airflow envelope, holds 55 unverified legacy rows in quarantine until cell-level NASA NTRS verification is complete, and lets users test out-of-domain ML refusal behavior.
  • Flame Vision (/vision) & Ask AURA (/ask): Inspects flame imagery with pixel-level luminous soot vs. blue emission splits and provides deterministic, page-cited answers from primary NASA NTRS documents.
  • Interactive 3D STEM Missions (/missions): Five hands-on chapters—including an interactive 3D BASS-II assembly tour and fault-repair mission—that teach students how airflow, buoyancy, and oxygen affect spacecraft fires.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • For researchers and mission planners: Separates verified flight observations from extrapolations, highlighting exact research gaps (such as high-O₂, reduced-pressure exploration atmospheres) before crews rely on incomplete assumptions.
  • For students and educators: Makes NASA’s technical combustion reports approachable through 3D visualization, fair-test comparisons, and falsifiable mission challenges.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

  • Frontend & 3D: Next.js 16 (App Router), React, TypeScript, CSS Modules, and Three.js (WebGL2 with custom GLSL particle shaders and OrbitControls, plus SVG fallbacks).
  • Validation & Science Engine: Shared TypeScript workspace packages (@astraflame/shared, @astraflame/science) with Zod schema validation, deterministic evidence retrieval, and Vitest unit tests.
  • Data Sources: Primary NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) publications and imagery from BASS, BASS-II, Saffire IV–VI, and LUCI.

Creativity & Design Considerations

Most AI or science apps try to look smart by answering every question—even when no data exists. Our team designed AstraFlame around scientific honesty first: we built explicit quarantine ledgers, out-of-domain abstention, and side-by-side fair-test checks right into the UI. We also separated Explorer mode (plain language for students) from Scientist mode (precision spinboxes, PDF page citations, and ML domain checks) so both audiences can use the same tool comfortably.
